question: What characteristics of God does the opening hymn bring together, and how does nature react to His presence?
The verb נָקַם (naqam, “avenge”) is repeated three times in verse 2: how should we read this language alongside “slow to anger” in verse 3?
How can the same God be “a stronghold in the day of distress” for some and “an overwhelming flood” for Nineveh?
Verse 15 speaks of “the feet of one who brings good news”: what news of relief could you bring to someone oppressed today?
What details of the battle and fall of Nineveh does the prophet describe, from the chariots to the pale faces?
What does the image of the lions' den, where no one frightened the cubs, say about the way Nineveh had lived?
The verb בָּזַז (bazaz, “plunder”) is spoken as a command: what does it mean that the city that plundered the peoples is now plundered?
“Behold, I am against you”: what kind of power, in our day, do you think needs to hear this phrase?
Of what sins is Nineveh accused in the first verses of the chapter?
Why does the prophet recall the fall of Thebes in Egypt when speaking to Nineveh?
The devouring insect יֶלֶק (yeleq, “young locust”) appears several times: what does this image say about the strength and the duration of the empire?
The book ends with a question: “who has not felt your endless cruelty?” How does the evil done by someone powerful affect many lives around them?
